To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the average value can be localized in a multi-class scatterplot, (2) the average value of a set can be localized more accurately when the average value of the set is higher, and (3) the average value is localized more accurately when using a salient encoding.

(1) people can quickly and accurately estimate the relative mean of a small set of points, (2) people are less accurate for larger sets of points, and (3) people are more accurate for more salient encodings, but less accurate for more redundant encodings.

(i) judgements are no harder with additional points, (ii) redundant and conflicting encodings have little effect on the task, (iii) additional sets do not affect judgements, and (iv) less salient encodings make the task more difficult.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how humans make judgements over large sets of data, and the implications for visualization design.
how the visual system aggregates information from a collection of visual objects, and what constraints this places on visualizations.
how humans perceive aggregate values, and how to design effective visualizations to support this task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no significant differences in the accuracy of mean value judgements for different numbers of points, different encodings of data, and different numbers of data sets.
the visual system is able to aggregate information in a way that is robust to the number of objects in the set and to the number of sets, as long as the encoding of the data is salient.
the visual system is capable of making highly accurate judgements over long time scales, but that this capability is highly sensitive to the design of the visualization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the case of scatterplots, we can make highly efficient judgements about the mean value of sets, but only when the encoding is highly salient and the sets are small.

the perception literature provides an excellent framework for understanding the performance of aggregate judgements in scatterplots, and the results of this study can be used as the basis of a new set of guidelines for the effective encoding of multiclass scatterplots.

the visual system is able to aggregate multiple values into a single summary, and that this summary is robust to the number of points and sets considered, as well as to redundant and conflicting encodings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual system is surprisingly robust to the presence of additional data, and the presence of conflicting encodings.
the visual system can aggregate data efficiently, and that this efficiency is not strongly affected by the complexity of the data.

, when the number of classes is small and the data is well-sampled, the visual system can make aggregate judgements about the data, and that the judgements are relatively robust to a number of common visualization techniques.
